title: Dido hospita. Aeneas se aperit
titleEn: Dido's Welcome; Aeneas Steps from the Cloud — Aeneid I.561–656
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Dido answers Ilioneus briefly, her face lowered. She tells the Trojans to lay fear aside: a hard necessity and a kingdom still new force her to post guards along her whole frontier, but who does not know the race of Aeneas and the story of Troy? Whether they want Italy or Sicily and King Acestes, she will send them off safe and help them; or they may settle with her, Trojan and Tyrian alike. She wishes Aeneas himself had been driven here by the same wind, and will send men along the coast and through Libya to search for him. Achates and Aeneas, who have been burning to break out of their cloud, hear her; Achates points out that the ships and men are safe, all but one drowned before their eyes, as Venus said. The cloud splits and melts away, and Aeneas stands revealed, like a god in face and shoulders, for his mother has breathed beauty on his hair and a youthful glow on his eyes. He tells the queen that he is the man they seek. He cannot repay her, who alone pities the leavings of Troy and takes them into her city and home; he prays the gods to do so, and promises that while rivers run, shadows move and heaven feeds the stars, her honour and name will last in every land he is called to. He greets Ilioneus, Serestus, Gyas and Cloanthus. Dido, stunned at the sight of him and at his fall, asks whether he is the Aeneas whom Venus bore to Anchises by the Simois. She remembers Teucer coming to Sidon, and since then she has known the fall of Troy, his name and the Greek kings. She welcomes the Trojans: fortune has tossed her too, and she has learnt to help the wretched. She leads Aeneas to the palace, orders sacrifice at the temples, and sends bulls, pigs and lambs to the ships, while the palace is made ready for a feast. Aeneas sends Achates to fetch Ascanius, with gifts rescued from Troy: Helen's robe and veil, Ilione's sceptre, a pearl necklace and a double crown.
part: Dido's Welcome; Aeneas Steps from the Cloud (I.561–656)

sentences.t: Tum breviter Dido, voltum demissa, profatur:
sentences.l: Then briefly Dido, her face cast down, speaks forth:
sentences.i: Then Dido, her face lowered, answers briefly:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Dido's first speech (562–578). 'voltum demissa' — 'lowered as to her face': a perfect passive participle with an accusative of respect, a Greek-style construction you will see constantly in Virgil. Greenough prints 'voltum' for 'vultum'. 'profatur' — historical present of the deponent 'profor'; the colon leads into the speech.

sentences.t: “Solvite corde metum, Teucri, secludite curas.
sentences.l: “Loosen from the heart your fear, Trojans, shut away your cares.
sentences.i: “Let the fear go from your hearts, Trojans, and put your troubles away.
sentences.n: 'corde' — ablative of separation (no preposition), singular because 'the heart' is each man's own. 'Teucri' — vocative plural, 'Trojans' (from their ancestor Teucer); the Greek eu is one syllable. Two imperatives, 'solvite' and 'secludite'; the second is literally 'shut away, shut out'.

sentences.t:
Res dura et regni novitas me talia cogunt
moliri, et late finis custode tueri.
sentences.l:
A hard situation and the newness of the kingdom force me such things
to attempt, and to guard the frontiers widely with a sentry.
sentences.i: A harsh situation and the youth of my realm drive me to take such precautions, and to post sentries along my frontiers from end to end.
sentences.n: 'Res dura et regni novitas' are the double subject of 'cogunt' (plural verb). 'me… moliri… tueri' — 'cogunt' takes an accusative and infinitive: 'force me to undertake, and to protect'. 'moliri' is deponent. 'finis' — accusative plural in -is, for 'fines'. 'custode' — ablative of means, singular for collective: 'with a guard'. 'late' — 'widely'. Dido explains why her coast guards turned the Trojans back (Ilioneus's complaint, 539–541).

sentences.t:
Quis genus Aeneadum, quis Troiae nesciat urbem,
virtutesque virosque, aut tanti incendia belli?
sentences.l:
Who would not know the race of the Aeneadae, who the city of Troy,
and its valours and its men, or the fires of so great a war?
sentences.i: Who is there that would not know the line of Aeneas, who the city of Troy, its heroism and its heroes, or the burning of a war so great?
sentences.n: 'Quis… nesciat' — a rhetorical question with the potential subjunctive: 'who would be ignorant?', i.e. nobody. 'Aeneadum' — genitive plural of 'Aeneadae', 'the followers of Aeneas', in the poets' -um for -arum (the ending you have met in 'superum', 'Danaum'); it has the syllables Ae-ne-a-dum, the middle e short before a vowel. 'virtutesque virosque' — 'both valours and men', with the double -que you will see constantly. 'tanti… belli' — genitive, agreeing: 'of so great a war'; 'incendia' are the fires of Troy's burning.

sentences.t:
Non obtusa adeo gestamus pectora Poeni,
nec tam aversus equos Tyria Sol iungit ab urbe.
sentences.l:
We Phoenicians do not carry hearts so blunted,
nor does the Sun yoke his horses so far turned from the Tyrian city.
sentences.i: We Carthaginians do not carry hearts so dull, and the Sun does not drive his team so far from our Tyrian city.
sentences.n: 'Poeni' — the Phoenicians, whose descendants the Carthaginians were (hence 'Punic'). 'obtusa… pectora' — 'blunted hearts': a figure from a dulled blade. 'gestamus' — 'we bear about'. 'aversus' — 'turned away', nominative with 'Sol', predicative: the Sun does not yoke 'turned away'. 'equos' — accusative plural. The sense, as commonly taken: we do not live at the world's remote edge, out of reach of the news of the age.

sentences.t:
Seu vos Hesperiam magnam Saturniaque arva,
sive Erycis finis regemque optatis Acesten,
auxilio tutos dimittam, opibusque iuvabo.
sentences.l:
Whether for great Hesperia and the Saturnian fields
or for the borders of Eryx and King Acestes you wish,
I will send you off made safe with an escort, and help you with my means.
sentences.i: Whether you are making for great Hesperia and the lands of Saturn, or for the borders of Eryx and King Acestes, I shall see you off safe with an escort and help you from my resources.
sentences.n: 'Seu… sive… optatis' — 'whether… or…': the one verb 'optatis' (you wish for) stands in the second half and serves both. 'Hesperiam' — 'the western land', Italy; 'Saturnia arva' — the fields of Saturn, who in legend had ruled in Italy. 'Erycis finis' — 'the borders of Eryx' (the mountain in western Sicily); 'finis' is accusative plural. 'auxilio' — ablative of means, here 'with an escort or aid'; 'tutos' is predicative, 'as safe men'.

sentences.t: Voltis et his mecum pariter considere regnis;
sentences.l: Do you wish also, with me, equally, to settle in these realms;
sentences.i: Do you also wish to settle with me, on equal terms, in these realms;
sentences.n: 'Voltis' — Greenough's spelling of 'vultis'; 'et' means 'also': 'do you also wish…?' 'considere' is the infinitive of 'consido', 'to settle down'. 'his… regnis' — ablative of place without a preposition. 'pariter' — 'equally, on equal terms'. The semicolon links to what follows.

sentences.t: urbem quam statuo vestra est, subducite navis;
sentences.l: the city which I found is yours; draw up the ships;
sentences.i: the city I am founding is yours; haul your ships ashore;
sentences.n: 'urbem quam statuo vestra est' — the antecedent has been drawn into the relative clause and takes its case, so 'urbem' is accusative although it is the subject of 'est' ('the city which I found, it is yours'); it is a common Latin arrangement. 'statuo' — 'I set up, found'. 'subducite navis' — 'draw up (on the beach)': 'navis' is accusative plural in -is.

sentences.t: Tros Tyriusque mihi nullo discrimine agetur.
sentences.l: Trojan and Tyrian will be handled by me with no distinction.
sentences.i: Trojan and Tyrian will be one to me, with no difference between them.
sentences.n: 'Tros Tyriusque' — 'both Trojan and Tyrian', two singular nouns for the two peoples, with the singular verb 'agetur'. 'agetur' — future passive of 'ago' in a sense like 'will be dealt with, treated'. 'nullo discrimine' — ablative of manner, 'with no distinction'. 'mihi' — dative of the person concerned, 'with me, in my eyes'; poets also put the agent in the dative with a passive verb, so 'by me' is possible.

sentences.t:
Atque utinam rex ipse Noto compulsus eodem
adforet Aeneas!
sentences.l:
And would that the king himself, driven by the same South wind,
were present, Aeneas!
sentences.i: And if only the king himself, driven by the same south wind, were here — Aeneas!
sentences.n: 'Atque utinam… adforet' — 'utinam' with the imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish about the present that cannot be fulfilled as things stand. 'adforet' is an old form of 'adesset' (the 'fore' forms, as 'forem' for 'essem'). 'Noto… eodem' — the same wind (Notus, the South wind) that drove the Trojans; 'compulsus' agrees with 'Aeneas'. The exclamation puts the name at the end.

sentences.t:
Equidem per litora certos
dimittam et Libyae lustrare extrema iubebo,
si quibus eiectus silvis aut urbibus errat.”
sentences.l:
Indeed along the shores trusty men
I will send off, and of Libya the farthest parts to search I shall order,
if in any woods or cities, cast out, he wanders.”
sentences.i: In truth, I shall send out dependable men along the shore and have them comb the farthest parts of Libya, in case he is wandering, cast out, in some forest or town.”
sentences.n: 'Equidem' — 'for my part, indeed', usually with a first-person verb. 'dimittam' — 'I will send off'; 'iubebo' takes an infinitive, 'lustrare', whose subject is the men just sent (understood). 'extrema' is a neuter plural noun, 'the far parts'. 'si quibus… silvis aut urbibus' — 'if in any woods or cities' (after 'si', 'quibus' means 'any'). 'eiectus' — 'thrown out' by the sea. The closing mark ends Dido's speech.

sentences.t:
His animum arrecti dictis et fortis Achates
et pater Aeneas iamdudum erumpere nubem
ardebant.
sentences.l:
Roused in spirit by these words, both brave Achates
and father Aeneas for some time to burst out of the cloud
had been burning.
sentences.i: Fired by these words, brave Achates and father Aeneas had both been longing for some time to burst out of the cloud.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'His animum arrecti dictis' — 'aroused as to their spirit by these words': 'animum' is the accusative of respect again, 'dictis' ablative of cause. 'arrecti' agrees with both subjects. 'iamdudum' with the imperfect 'ardebant' — 'had been burning for a long time already'. 'erumpere nubem' — the infinitive with an accusative object, 'to break out of (burst through) the cloud'. The cloud is the mist Venus put round them at I.411 ff. 'pater' is a standing title of respect for Aeneas.

sentences.t: Prior Aenean compellat Achates:
sentences.l: First Achates addresses Aeneas:
sentences.i: Achates is first to speak to Aeneas:
sentences.n: 'Prior' — an adjective used as an adverb, 'first'. 'Aenean' — Greek accusative. 'compellat' — 'addresses'. The colon opens Achates's short speech.

sentences.t: “Nate dea, quae nunc animo sententia surgit?
sentences.l: “Goddess-born, what resolve now rises in your mind?
sentences.i: “Son of a goddess, what purpose is rising in your mind now?
sentences.n: 'Nate dea' — vocative 'nate', with 'dea' ablative of origin: 'born from a goddess'. 'animo' — ablative of place without 'in' ('in your mind'); 'surgit' — 'rises up'. 'quae sententia' — 'what purpose'.

sentences.t: omnia tuta vides, classem sociosque receptos.
sentences.l: You see everything safe: the fleet and companions recovered.
sentences.i: You see everything safe, the fleet and our friends recovered.
sentences.n: 'omnia tuta vides' — 'tuta' is predicative with 'omnia'. 'receptos' — the participle agrees with 'sociosque' (the nearer noun), but belongs to 'classem' too. Achates is reporting what Venus promised at I.390 (comrades and fleet restored), now borne out by the sight of Ilioneus and the others.

sentences.t:
Unus abest, medio in fluctu quem vidimus ipsi
submersum;
sentences.l:
One is missing, whom in the middle of the wave we ourselves
saw sunk;
sentences.i: One alone is missing, whom we ourselves watched go under in the midst of the waves;
sentences.n: 'Unus abest' — the missing man is taken to be Orontes, whose ship was swallowed by the sea at I.113–117. 'quem vidimus ipsi submersum' — 'whom we saw (as) sunk': the participle is predicative. 'ipsi' — 'we ourselves', so there can be no doubt.

sentences.t: dictis respondent cetera matris.”
sentences.l: the rest answers to the words of your mother.”
sentences.i: all else bears out your mother's words.”
sentences.n: 'dictis respondent cetera matris' — 'the other things answer to the words of your mother'; 'cetera' is neuter plural, the subject of the plural verb. 'respondent' means 'correspond, tally with'. The words are Venus's at I.390 ff.: his comrades and fleet would return. The closing mark ends Achates's speech.

sentences.t:
Vix ea fatus erat, cum circumfusa repente
scindit se nubes et in aethera purgat apertum.
sentences.l:
Scarcely had he said these things, when poured round suddenly
the cloud splits itself and clears away into the open air.
sentences.i: Scarcely had he spoken when the cloud about them parted all at once, and melted away into the open sky.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Vix ea fatus erat, cum' — 'scarcely had he said these things when': the 'cum' clause carries the main event, so it takes the indicative. 'fatus erat' — pluperfect of the deponent 'for'. 'scindit se' — a reflexive where English would say 'is torn apart'; 'circumfusa' — 'poured around'. 'in aethera purgat apertum' — 'clears into the open air'; 'purgat' is used intransitively, with the cloud as subject.

sentences.t:
Restitit Aeneas claraque in luce refulsit,
os umerosque deo similis;
sentences.l:
Aeneas stood and shone out in the clear light,
like a god in face and shoulders;
sentences.i: Aeneas stood still and shone out in the bright light, like a god in face and shoulders;
sentences.n: 'Restitit… refulsit' — two perfects: he stopped, and shone. 'os umerosque deo similis' — accusative of respect with 'similis': 'like a god as to face and shoulders', and 'deo' is the dative after 'similis'. 'clara in luce' — in the clear daylight, now that the cloud is gone.

sentences.t:
namque ipsa decoram
caesariem nato genetrix lumenque iuventae
purpureum et laetos oculis adflarat honores:
sentences.l:
for she herself, the comely
hair to her son, his mother, and the glow of youth
purple, and glad graces on his eyes had breathed:
sentences.i: for his mother herself had breathed upon her son beautiful hair, the bright bloom of youth, and a joyous charm in his eyes:
sentences.n: 'namque' explains the god-like look. 'adflarat' is the contracted form of 'adflaverat', pluperfect; 'ipsa genetrix' is Venus. 'purpureum' is used of light and brightness, not just colour (a 'shining' youth). 'oculis' — 'in his eyes' (dative or ablative of place); 'laetos honores' — 'glad adornments', that is grace. The colon leads into a comparison.

sentences.t:
quale manus addunt ebori decus, aut ubi flavo
argentum Pariusve lapis circumdatur auro.
sentences.l:
as hands add beauty to ivory, or when with yellow
gold silver or Parian stone is encircled.
sentences.i: as when craftsmen's hands lend ivory its beauty, or when silver, or marble from Paros, is set round with yellow gold.
sentences.n: A short simile with 'quale' standing without its correlative 'tale'. 'manus' — 'hands' for the craftsman's skill. 'ubi' with the present: 'or when'. 'Pariusve lapis' — the marble of the island of Paros. 'circumdatur' is the passive: the silver or the marble is encircled by the gold ('auro', ablative of means).

sentences.t:
Tum sic reginam adloquitur, cunctisque repente
improvisus ait:
sentences.l:
Then thus he addresses the queen, and to all suddenly
unforeseen he says:
sentences.i: Then he speaks to the queen thus, and, appearing without warning to them all, says:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Aeneas's speech (595–610). 'adloquitur' is a historical present, deponent. 'improvisus' — 'unforeseen' (as the one who appears), predicative, with 'cunctis' dative. 'repente' — suddenly. The colon introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
“Coram, quem quaeritis, adsum,
Troius Aeneas, Lybicis ereptus ab undis.
sentences.l:
“Here, whom you seek, I am present,
Trojan Aeneas, snatched from the Libyan waves.
sentences.i: “Look, I stand before you, the man you seek: Aeneas of Troy, plucked from the Libyan waves.
sentences.n: 'Coram' — 'in person, face to face'. 'quem quaeritis' — 'whom you seek', a relative clause standing in apposition to the subject of 'adsum'; 'Troius Aeneas' is in apposition too. 'Troius' is the adjective ('Trojan') and has three syllables here. 'ereptus' — 'snatched away', hence 'rescued'.

sentences.t:
O sola infandos Troiae miserata labores,
quae nos, reliquias Danaum, terraeque marisque
omnibus exhaustos iam casibus, omnium egenos,
urbe, domo, socias,
sentences.l:
O you alone who pitied the unspeakable labours of Troy,
you who us, the remnant of the Danaans, of land and sea
by all misfortunes now worn out, in want of everything,
associate with your city, your home,
sentences.i: You alone have pitied the unspeakable sufferings of Troy; you take us in, the remnant the Greeks left, spent by every kind of hardship on land and sea and stripped of everything, to share your city and your home.
sentences.n: The long period is built on a vocative: 'O sola… miserata' (the participle of the deponent 'miseror', 'pity', agreeing with 'sola'). 'infandos' — 'unspeakable'. 'quae nos… socias' — 'you who associate us…': 'socias' is the second singular of 'socio', and its objects, 'nos reliquias Danaum', are glossed by two participial phrases. 'reliquias Danaum' — 'the remnant of the Danaans' (the poets' genitive plural in -um); the first syllable of 'reliquias' is long in verse. 'terraeque marisque' — genitive of 'terra' and 'mare', both with 'casibus'. 'omnium egenos' — 'in need of all things', the adjective with a genitive. 'urbe, domo' — ablatives, 'in your city, your home'.

sentences.t:
grates persolvere dignas
non opis est nostrae, Dido, nec quicquid ubique est
gentis Dardaniae, magnum quae sparsa per orbem.
sentences.l:
worthy thanks to pay back
is not within our means, Dido, nor of whatever there is anywhere
of the Dardan nation, which is scattered through the great world.
sentences.i: To repay you thanks as you deserve is beyond our power, Dido, and beyond the power of whatever is left of the Dardan race, wherever it lies scattered over the wide world.
sentences.n: 'grates persolvere dignas non opis est nostrae' — the infinitive phrase is the subject; 'opis nostrae' is a predicate genitive, 'it is not of our power'. 'grates' is a noun found only in the plural, 'thanks' (accusative). 'nec quicquid ubique est gentis Dardaniae' — 'nor [is it of the power of] whatever there is anywhere of the Dardan people'. 'quae sparsa' — 'which is scattered', with 'quae' referring to the people.

sentences.t:
Di tibi, si qua pios respectant numina, si quid
usquam iustitia est et mens sibi conscia recti,
praemia digna ferant.
sentences.l:
Gods to you, if any divine powers look on the dutiful, if anything
anywhere of justice there is, and a mind to itself aware of right,
worthy rewards may they bring.
sentences.i: May the gods grant you your due reward, if the powers of heaven take any heed of the dutiful, if there is any justice anywhere, and a conscience sure of its own uprightness.
sentences.n: 'Di tibi… praemia digna ferant' — an optative (wishing) subjunctive, 'may they bring'. 'Di' is the contracted nominative plural of 'deus'. 'si qua… numina respectant' and 'si quid… iustitia est' — two conditions, offered as hope; 'pios' means those who do their duty to gods, kin and guests. 'mens sibi conscia recti' — 'a mind conscious to itself of the right', the genitive 'recti' with 'conscia'.

sentences.t:
Quae te tam laeta tulerunt
saecula?
sentences.l:
What so happy bore you
ages?
sentences.i: What ages, so blest, brought you into the world?
sentences.n: 'Quae… saecula' — 'saecula' is the neuter plural, 'what ages', so 'tulerunt' is plural. The question is exclamatory and rhetorical, praise in the form of astonishment. 'te tulerunt' — 'bore you'.

sentences.t: Qui tanti talem genuere parentes?
sentences.l: What parents of such stature begot such a one?
sentences.i: What parents, so great, brought forth a woman like you?
sentences.n: 'Qui tanti talem genuere parentes' — 'genuere' is the third plural perfect '-ere' for '-erunt', which you will see constantly. 'tanti' agrees with 'parentes', 'talem' is the object: 'such parents, such a daughter'.

sentences.t:
In freta dum fluvii current, dum montibus umbrae
lustrabunt convexa, polus dum sidera pascet,
semper honos nomenque tuum laudesque manebunt,
quae me cumque vocant terrae.
sentences.l:
As long as rivers into the seas run, as long as on the mountains shadows
will range over the hollows, as long as heaven feeds the stars,
always your honour and name and praises will remain,
whatever lands call me.”
sentences.i: So long as streams flow seaward, so long as shadows pass over the hollows of the hills, so long as the sky pastures the stars, your honour and your name and your praise will abide, whatever lands may summon me.”
sentences.n: A vow of everlasting memory in a series of 'dum' clauses; 'dum' with the future ('current', 'lustrabunt', 'pascet') means 'so long as'. 'polus' — the vault of heaven. 'montibus' — ablative of place, 'on the mountains'; 'convexa' — neuter plural, 'the hollows' (ancient commentators differ: valleys or slopes). The closing mark ends Aeneas's speech (see the next unit for where the edition prints it). The main clause comes after: the plural verb 'manebunt' agrees with three subjects ('honos nomenque tuum laudesque'). 'quae me cumque vocant terrae' is a tmesis, the splitting of the word 'quaecumque' by the insertion of 'me': 'whatever lands call me'.

sentences.t:
”Sic fatus, amicum
Ilionea petit dextra, laevaque Serestum,
post alios, fortemque Gyan fortemque Cloanthum.
sentences.l:
Having thus spoken, he seeks his friend
Ilioneus with his right hand, and Serestus with his left,
after the others, brave Gyas and brave Cloanthus.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and reached out, his right hand to his friend Ilioneus, his left to Serestus, and then to the others, brave Gyas and brave Cloanthus.
sentences.n: The closing speech mark of Aeneas is printed in Greenough's text after a space and glued to 'Sic' ('terrae. ”Sic'), so the mark heads this unit's `t`; it is carried in the `l` and `i` of the previous unit, where the speech ends. 'Sic fatus' — 'having thus spoken', the perfect participle of the deponent 'for'. 'petit' — 'seeks', here 'reaches for'. 'Ilionea… Gyan' — Greek accusatives. 'dextra… laevaque' — ablatives of means. 'fortem… fortemque' — the double -que once more.

sentences.t:
Obstipuit primo aspectu Sidonia Dido,
casu deinde viri tanto, et sic ore locuta est:
sentences.l:
Sidonian Dido was stunned at first sight,
then at the man's so great calamity, and thus with her mouth spoke:
sentences.i: Sidonian Dido was struck dumb, first by the sight of him, then by the great misfortune of the man, and she spoke thus:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Obstipuit' — perfect of 'obstipesco', 'was stunned'. 'primo aspectu' — ablative of cause; 'casu… tanto' likewise. 'Sidonia' — 'of Sidon', a Phoenician city, so 'Phoenician'. 'locuta est' — perfect of the deponent 'loquor'; the colon opens Dido's second speech (615–630).

sentences.t:
“Quis te, nate dea, per tanta pericula casus
insequitur?
sentences.l:
“What chance, goddess-born, through such perils
pursues you?
sentences.i: “What fortune, son of a goddess, hounds you through such dangers?
sentences.n: 'Quis… casus' — 'quis' for 'qui', as an adjective with 'casus'. 'nate dea' — the same vocative as Achates used at 582. 'insequitur' — the compound verb, 'pursues'.

sentences.t: Quae vis immanibus applicat oris?
sentences.l: What force brings you to savage shores?
sentences.i: What power drives you ashore on this wild coast?
sentences.n: 'applicat' — 'puts you in, drives you up to'; 'immanibus… oris' is dative, 'savage' (strictly: monstrous, beyond measure).

sentences.t:
Tune ille Aeneas, quem Dardanio Anchisae
alma Venus Phrygii genuit Simoentis ad undam?
sentences.l:
Are you that Aeneas, whom to Dardanian Anchises
nurturing Venus bore by the wave of Phrygian Simois?
sentences.i: Can you be that Aeneas whom kindly Venus bore to Anchises of Dardanus's line, by the stream of the Phrygian Simois?
sentences.n: 'Tune' — 'tu' + enclitic '-ne' (a yes-or-no question). 'ille Aeneas' — 'that famous Aeneas'. 'Dardanio Anchisae' — dative with 'genuit': 'bore to Dardan Anchises' (a Dardanian, that is a Trojan, by descent). The verse scans only if the -o of 'Dardanio' is not elided before 'Anchisae': a hiatus, with the long vowel kept. 'alma Venus' — 'nourishing Venus', a standing epithet. 'Simoentis' is the Greek genitive of Simois, the Trojan river, in four syllables (Si-mo-en-tis).

sentences.i: And in truth I remember that Teucer came to Sidon, driven from his homeland, seeking a new kingdom with the help of Belus;
sentences.n: 'memini' takes an accusative and infinitive: 'I remember Teucer (to) come'; 'Teucrum' is the accusative of Teucer, with Greek eu in one syllable. This is the Greek Teucer, son of Telamon, exiled by his father, who is said to have founded Salamis in Cyprus. 'Sidona' — Greek accusative. 'finibus… patriis' — ablative of separation, 'from his native borders'. 'auxilio Beli' — 'with the help of Belus', ablative of means; Belus is Dido's father.

sentences.t:
genitor tum Belus opimam
vastabat Cyprum, et victor dicione tenebat.
sentences.l:
my father Belus then the rich
Cyprus was laying waste, and as victor held it in his power.
sentences.i: my father Belus was then ravaging wealthy Cyprus, and held it, victorious, under his rule.
sentences.n: 'genitor tum Belus' — Dido speaks of her own father. 'vastabat… tenebat' — two imperfects. 'dicione' — ablative, 'under his sway'. 'victor' is a noun used as an adjective (predicative), 'as victor'.

sentences.t:
Tempore iam ex illo casus mihi cognitus urbis
Troianae nomenque tuum regesque Pelasgi.
sentences.l:
From that time already the fate was known to me of the city
Trojan, and your name, and the Pelasgian kings.
sentences.i: From that time on I have known the fall of the Trojan city, and your name, and the Greek kings.
sentences.n: 'Tempore iam ex illo' — 'from that time already'. 'casus' is the subject with 'nomen' and 'reges'; 'cognitus' agrees with the first of them, 'casus' ('est' is understood). 'mihi' is a dative of the agent with the perfect participle: 'known by me'. 'Pelasgi' — the Pelasgians are an old name for the Greeks.

sentences.t:
Ipse hostis Teucros insigni laude ferebat,
seque ortum antiqua Teucrorum ab stirpe volebat.
sentences.l:
He himself, an enemy, used to raise the Teucrians with distinguished praise,
and wished himself sprung from the ancient stock of the Teucrians.
sentences.i: He himself, though their enemy, used to extol the Trojans with high praise, and wished to be thought a scion of the ancient Teucrian stock.
sentences.n: 'Ipse hostis' — 'he himself, although an enemy': Belus. 'ferebat' — 'carried up, extolled'. 'Teucros' — 'Teucri', the Trojans, named from their early king Teucer (not the Greek Teucer of 619); the Greek eu is one syllable. 'seque ortum… volebat' — 'se' is the subject of an understood 'esse': 'wished himself to be sprung', that is, to be thought a descendant. The Greek Teucer was Trojan on his mother's side (his mother, Hesione, was a daughter of Laomedon).

sentences.t: Quare agite, O tectis, iuvenes, succedite nostris.
sentences.l: Wherefore come, O young men, step into our dwellings.
sentences.i: So come, young men, and enter beneath our roof.
sentences.n: 'Quare agite' — 'therefore come on' (the imperative of 'ago', used as an exhortation). 'succedite' — 'go up into' with the dative 'tectis nostris'. 'tectis' means 'roofs, houses'. 'O' is printed before 'tectis' but goes with 'iuvenes'; the final -e of 'agite' elides before it.

sentences.t:
Me quoque per multos similis fortuna labores
iactatam hac demum voluit consistere terra.
sentences.l:
Me also a like fortune through many labours
wished to settle, tossed about, in this land at last.
sentences.i: A like fortune has tossed me too through many hardships, and willed that I should come to rest at last in this land.
sentences.n: 'Me quoque… iactatam… voluit consistere' — 'voluit' takes the accusative-and-infinitive: 'wished me, tossed about, to settle'. 'similis fortuna' — 'a like fortune', the subject. 'hac demum terra' — 'in this land at last'; 'consistere' — 'to come to rest'.

sentences.t: Non ignara mali, miseris succurrere disco.”
sentences.l: Not ignorant of evil, to come to the aid of the wretched I learn.”
sentences.i: I have known suffering myself, and so I am learning to help the suffering.”
sentences.n: 'Non ignara mali' — 'not ignorant of evil': a litotes (an understatement by negation) with the genitive 'mali' after 'ignara', agreeing with Dido herself. 'miseris succurrere' — dative with the infinitive; 'disco' — 'I learn', a present that suggests a lesson still going on. The closing mark ends Dido's speech.

sentences.t: Sic memorat;
sentences.l: So she speaks;
sentences.i: So she speaks;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sic memorat' — 'thus she says', the verb of narration after a speech, a historical present. The semicolon joins two simultaneous actions with 'simul… simul'.

sentences.t:
simul Aenean in regia ducit
tecta, simul divom templis indicit honorem.
sentences.l:
at the same time she leads Aeneas into the royal
house, at the same time proclaims honour at the temples of the gods.
sentences.i: at once she leads Aeneas into her royal house, and at once proclaims worship in the temples of the gods.
sentences.n: 'simul… simul' — 'at the same time… at the same time'. 'Aenean' — Greek accusative. 'in regia… tecta' — 'regia' is an adjective, neuter plural, with 'tecta'. 'divom' — old genitive plural of 'divus' ('god'), with 'templis' (ablative of place without 'in', 'at the temples'; some take it as dative). 'indicit honorem' — 'proclaims an honour', that is, orders sacrifice.

sentences.t:
Nec minus interea sociis ad litora mittit
viginti tauros, magnorum horrentia centum
terga suum, pinguis centum cum matribus agnos,
munera laetitiamque dii.
sentences.l:
No less meanwhile to the companions on the shore she sends
twenty bulls, of great swine a hundred bristling
backs, a hundred fat lambs with their mothers,
gifts and the gladness of the god (or of the day).
sentences.i: Meanwhile she sends no less to her comrades on the shore: twenty bulls, a hundred bristling backs of great swine, a hundred fat lambs with their mothers, gifts, and good cheer besides.
sentences.n: 'Nec minus' — 'and none the less'. 'sociis ad litora' — 'to the companions at the shore'. 'terga suum' — 'backs of pigs', the part for the whole (a poetic way of counting animals); 'suum' is the genitive plural of 'sus'. 'pinguis… agnos' — accusative plural in -is. 'munera laetitiamque dii' — the line is a half-line, one of the places where Virgil left a verse unfinished. The last word is uncertain: 'dii' may be an old genitive of 'dies' ('the gladness of the day', the feast day) or a spelling of 'dei' ('of the god', Bacchus, so wine). The English keeps both open.

sentences.t:
At domus interior regali splendida luxu
instruitur, mediisque parant convivia tectis:
sentences.l:
But the inner house, splendid with royal luxury,
is being fitted out, and in the middle of the palace they prepare a feast:
sentences.i: But within, the palace is being furnished in royal splendour, and in its central halls a banquet is made ready:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'domus interior' — 'the inner house'. 'regali… luxu' — ablative of cause or respect with 'splendida': 'bright with royal luxury'. 'instruitur' — present passive. 'parant' — an indefinite plural, 'they prepare', i.e. the servants. 'mediis tectis' — 'in the midst of the house', ablative of place. The colon introduces a list of the furnishings.

sentences.t:
arte laboratae vestes ostroque superbo,
ingens argentum mensis, caelataque in auro
fortia facta patrum, series longissima rerum
per tot ducta viros antiqua ab origine gentis.
sentences.l:
hangings worked with art, and in proud purple,
huge silver on the tables, and engraved in gold
the brave deeds of the fathers, a very long series of events
drawn through so many men from the ancient origin of the race.
sentences.i: There are hangings wrought with skill and splendid purple, great silver on the tables, and engraved in gold the brave deeds of their ancestors, a very long chain of exploits running through so many heroes from the ancient beginning of the people.
sentences.n: The list is a set of nominatives with no verb, taken from 'instruitur' above; the construction is loose but clear. 'arte laboratae vestes ostroque superbo' — 'cloths worked with art, and with proud purple' ('ostro' ablative of the dye). 'mensis' — dative or ablative, 'on the tables'. 'caelata… in auro' — 'engraved in gold' (on gold plate). 'series longissima rerum… ducta' — 'a very long chain of events, drawn through so many men'. 'patrum' — 'of the fathers' (ancestors).

sentences.i: Aeneas — for a father's love would not let his mind rest — sends swift Achates on ahead to the ships, to take the news to Ascanius and to bring the boy himself to the city;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The parenthesis 'neque enim… amor' contains 'passus' with 'est' understood: the perfect of the deponent 'patior', 'allowed'; 'consistere mentem' is accusative and infinitive after it, 'to rest, settle'. 'patrius amor' — an adjective, 'paternal love'. 'rapidum… Achaten' — Greek accusative, 'swift'. 'ferat… ducat' — the subjunctives express purpose or command without 'ut', a common idiom. 'Ascanio' is the dative of the person to whom he carries 'haec'. 'ad moenia' — 'to the walls'.

sentences.t: omnis in Ascanio cari stat cura parentis.
sentences.l: All the care of the dear parent rests in Ascanius.
sentences.i: The whole concern of a loving father stands fixed on Ascanius.
sentences.n: 'omnis… cura' is the subject, 'omnis' is nominative feminine singular. 'in Ascanio stat' — 'rests on Ascanius'. 'cari… parentis' — genitive, 'of the dear father'.

sentences.t:
Munera praeterea, Iliacis erepta ruinis,
ferre iubet, pallam signis auroque rigentem,
et circumtextum croceo velamen acantho,
sentences.l:
Gifts besides, snatched from the ruins of Ilium,
he orders him to bring: a mantle stiff with figures and gold,
and a veil woven round with saffron acanthus,
sentences.i: He also orders him to bring gifts saved from the wreck of Troy: a robe stiff with figures and gold, and a veil bordered all round with yellow acanthus,
sentences.n: 'Munera… erepta' — neuter plural. 'ferre iubet' — 'iubeo' with the infinitive; the subject of 'ferre' (Achates) is understood. 'pallam signis auroque rigentem' — 'stiff with embroidered figures and gold'. 'circumtextum… croceo… acantho' — 'woven round with saffron acanthus': the acanthus is the stylized leaf pattern, in a saffron colour. 'velamen' — 'a covering, veil'.

sentences.t:
ornatus Argivae Helenae, quos illa Mycenis,
Pergama cum peteret inconcessosque hymenaeos,
extulerat, matris Ledae mirabile donum:
sentences.l:
the ornaments of Argive Helen, which she from Mycenae,
when she was making for Pergamum and the forbidden marriage,
had carried off, her mother Leda's marvellous gift:
sentences.i: They were the finery of Argive Helen, which she had brought away from Mycenae when she went to Troy and her unlawful marriage: a wonderful present from her mother Leda:
sentences.n: The gifts are glossed in apposition: 'ornatus' (accusative plural, fourth declension) 'Argivae Helenae'. 'Argivae' — 'of Argos', i.e. Greek. 'quos illa… extulerat' — pluperfect, 'she had carried out'. 'Mycenis' — 'from Mycenae' without a preposition; Virgil gives the Greek city, though Helen was Menelaus's wife, from Sparta. 'cum peteret' — imperfect subjunctive with 'cum', temporal-circumstantial. 'inconcessos hymenaeos' — 'hymenaeos' is the Greek noun in an accusative plural in -os; 'forbidden wedding' (Helen's union with Paris). 'mirabile donum' — apposition.

sentences.t:
praeterea sceptrum, Ilione quod gesserat olim,
maxima natarum Priami, colloque monile
bacatum, et duplicem gemmis auroque coronam.
sentences.l:
Besides, a sceptre, which Ilione had once carried,
the eldest of Priam's daughters, and a necklace for the neck
of pearls, and a double crown of gems and gold.
sentences.i: And also a sceptre that Ilione, Priam's eldest daughter, had once borne; a necklace of pearls for the throat; and a double crown of gems and gold.
sentences.n: 'Ilione' — a Greek nominative, the eldest daughter of Priam. 'quod gesserat' — 'which she had carried'. 'maxima natarum Priami' — 'greatest of Priam's daughters', that is the eldest; 'natarum' is the genitive plural. 'collo… monile bacatum' — 'a necklace set with berries (pearls)', the adjective from 'bacca'; 'collo' is a dative of reference, 'for the neck'. 'duplicem… coronam' — 'a double crown': the exact sense is uncertain (twofold, of gems and of gold, is the usual view); 'gemmis auroque' are ablatives.

sentences.t: Haec celerans ita ad naves tendebat Achates.
sentences.l: Hurrying these things, thus to the ships Achates was making his way.
sentences.i: So, hastening these tasks, Achates was making for the ships.
sentences.n: 'Haec celerans' — 'speeding these things', i.e. carrying out the task quickly. 'ita' — thus, as ordered. 'tendebat' — imperfect, 'was proceeding'.
